translation_en:
Chen Zhao 陳昭 (registered in a civilian household in Fengcheng County 豐城縣, Nanchang Prefecture 南昌府, Jiangxi; [two illegible characters]; specialized in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Yumin 育民; seventeenth in seniority among his male cousins; aged twenty-five, born on the thirteenth day of the ninth month). His great-grandfather was Chen Yongzhen 用貞, his grandfather was Chen Deheng 德衡, his father was Chen Lizhang 立章, his mother was née Li 黎, and his stepmother was née Li 李. Both his parents are deceased. His elder brother is Chen Yuhong 育弘, and his younger brothers are Chen Jiao 郊 and Chen Zhi 職. He is married to a woman née Lai 賴. He placed 42nd in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 188th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Jun 劉濬 (a native of Xingan County 新淦縣, Jiangxi, registered in a civilian household in Shangjin County 上津縣, Huguang; a student of the Directorate of Education (Guozisheng); specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu); courtesy name Yuanshen 淵深; fourth in seniority; aged twenty-nine, born on the eleventh day of the twelfth month). His great-grandfather was Liu Siqi 思齊, his grandfather was Liu Jili 季勵, his father is Liu Youmin 牖民 (Prefectural Director of Studies), and his mother is née Mao 毛. Both his parents are living. His elder brothers are Liu Yuanlie 源冽 (student of the Directorate of Education), Liu Yuanpei 源沛, and Liu Yuanqing 源清, and his younger brother is Liu Yuanhao 源浩. He is married to a woman née Jin 金. He placed 3rd in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 222nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Xixian 吳希賢 (registered in a civilian household in Putian County 莆田縣, Xinghua Prefecture 興化府, Fujian; an Added Student of the prefectural school; specialized in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Xixian 希賢; first in seniority; aged twenty-eight, born on the fifteenth day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Wu Fu 富, his grandfather is Wu Hong 洪, his father is Wu Xiong 熊, and his mother is née Huang 黃. Both his parents and grandparents are living. His younger brother is Wu Xiheng 希亨. He is married to a woman née Song 宋. He placed 32nd in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 45th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Wen 趙文 (registered in a military household in Shan Subprefecture 陝州, Henan Prefecture 河南府, Henan; a student of the Directorate of Education; specialized in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Mengzhang 孟章; first in seniority; aged twenty-seven, born on the tenth day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Zhao Sanweng 三翁, his grandfather was Zhao Lin 麟, his father is Zhao Xi 錫 (Diviner [Dianshu] in the princely establishment of Yiyang 義陽 [?]), his mother was née Wang 王, and his stepmother is née Liang 梁. Both his father and stepmother are living. His younger brothers are Zhao Wu 武 (Director of the Cuisine Service [Dianshan] in the princely establishment of Yiyang), Zhao Wei 威, and Zhao Ru 儒. He is married to a woman née Niu 牛. He placed [illegible] in the Henan Provincial Examination and [illegible] in the [Metropolitan Examination].

translation_en:
Yuan Chengde 袁成德: Registered in an official household in Jiading County, Suzhou Prefecture, Zhili; a Student of Astronomy in the Directorate of Astronomy, specializing in the Book of Documents (Shujing); courtesy name Yizhi, third in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty, born on the fourth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Yuan Guangda (Battalion Commander in the Yuan dynasty); his grandfather was Yuan Yanhe; his father was Yuan Shi (Erudite in the Directorate of Astronomy); and his mother is née Li. His mother is living. His elder brothers are Sizong and Qingzong, and his younger brother is Chang; he is married to Lady Wang. He placed 66th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 214th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Kuan 於寬: A native of Wujin County, Zhili, registered in an artisan household in the Construction Office of the Princely Establishment of Shu in Sichuan; a Student of the Directorate of Education, specializing in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Deyu, third in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty-two, born on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Yu Juetong; his grandfather was Yu Juefu; his father was Yu Shanliang; and his mother is née Gao. His mother is living. His elder brothers are Xian and Hong, and his younger brothers are Xuan and Ding; he married Lady Liu, and remarried to Lady Qian. He placed 20th in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 227th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Fang 史芳: Registered in a commoner household in Yi Subprefecture, Baoding Prefecture, Zhili; a Subprefectural Student, specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu); courtesy name Shixin, second in seniority among his brothers, aged twenty-eight, born on the twelfth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Shi Qigong; his grandfather was Shi Gang; his father is Shi Tai (Vice Commander of a Warden's Office); and his mother is née Zhang. Both of his parents are living. His elder brother is Mao, and his younger brothers are Ying, Lan, Zhen, and Fan; he is married to Lady Zheng. He placed 58th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 121st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Xuan 朱萱: Registered in a commoner household in Kunshan County, Suzhou Prefecture, Zhili; a Student of the Directorate of Education, specializing in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Shuzhi, fourth in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty-two, born on the thirtieth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Zhu Tianyou; his grandfather was Zhu Xian; his father is Zhu Zhen; his mother was née Zou, and his stepmother is née Wu. Both his father and stepmother are living. His elder brothers are Qin (a tribute student of the guiyou year [1453]), Hui, and Yun, and his younger brothers are Ju, Fu, and Ling (or Fuling); he married Lady He, and remarried to Lady Xia. He placed 139th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 158th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zheng Jie 鄭節 (courtesy name Congjian 從儉, twenty-fourth in seniority among his male cousins, aged thirty-five, born on the twenty-fifth day of the intercalary twelfth month) was registered in a commoner household in Guixi County 貴溪縣, Guangxin Prefecture 廣信府, Jiangxi 江西. He was a student of the Directorate of Education (Guozisheng) specializing in the Record of Rites (Liji). His great-grandfather was Zheng Boming 伯銘, his grandfather was Zheng Jixian 季顯, his father was Zheng Qi 祺 (Assistant Prefect), and his mother was née Jiang 江氏. His father was living and his mother deceased. He had an elder brother, Zheng Ding 鼎, and younger brothers, Zheng Fu 孚 and Zheng Xun 巽, and was married to a woman née Peng 彭氏. He placed fifty-third in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and two hundred and sixteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Jun 劉俊 (courtesy name Shiyong 時用, second in seniority, aged thirty, born on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month) was registered in a commoner household in Shunyi County 順義縣, Shuntian Prefecture 順天府. He was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing). His great-grandfather was Liu Dagong 大恭, his grandfather was Liu Yi 義, his father was Liu Qing 清, and his mother was née Zhang 張氏. Both his parents and grandparents were living. He had an elder brother, Liu Jie 傑, and a younger brother, Liu Jia 佳, and was married to a woman née Yuan 袁氏. He placed thirty-second in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and one hundred and fourteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jiang Chun 江純 (courtesy name Xiwen 希文, third in seniority, aged thirty-six, born on the sixteenth day of the ninth month) was registered in a commoner household in Fenghua County 奉化縣, Ningbo Prefecture 寧波府, Zhejiang 浙江. He was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing). His great-grandfather was Jiang Huanzong 煥宗, his grandfather was Jiang Shangda 尚達, his father was Jiang Xu 頊, and his mother was née Su 蘇氏. His mother was living and his father deceased. He had elder brothers, Jiang Hui 徽 and Jiang Lun 綸, and younger brothers, Jiang Ren 紉, Jiang Yi 彝, Jiang Zi 緇, Jiang Jiu 糾, Jiang Shou 綬, and Jiang Jin 紟, and was married to a woman née Zhou 周氏. He placed fifty-ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundred and seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Ding 郭鼎 (courtesy name Yuxuan 玉鉉, second in seniority, aged thirty-seven, born on the sixth day of the twelfth month) was registered in a commoner household in Wucheng County 武城縣, Dongchang Prefecture 東昌府, Shandong 山東. He was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents (Shujing). His great-grandfather was Guo Xineng 希能, his grandfather was Guo Sheng 勝, his father was Guo Yong 顒 (Department Magistrate), and his mother was née Liu 劉氏. His mother was living and his father deceased. He had an elder brother, Guo Yu 玉, and was married to a woman née Yin 尹氏. He placed thirty-first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and two hundred and fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
彭教
臣對臣聞大學有曰自天子以至於庶人壹是
皆以脩身為本蓋大學條目有八而脩身居其
中格物致知誠意正心皆所以脩其身者而
齊家治國平天下非本之脩身則無以成其功
也大哉身乎體斯道而行萬化其在此乎故曾
子一傳而子思則曰脩身則道立再傳而孟子
則曰脩其身而天下平然則聖賢道學相傳固
莫切於脩身而帝王治國平天下之道抑豈有
出於脩身之外者哉恭惟
===
皇上出震繼離嗣大歷服龍飛虎變御極當天聖作
神興萬物咸覩舜承堯志首行四罪之投武纘
文謨益隆周召之任屏耳目之玩弛不急之營
凡天下之所欲而未興所病而未除者以次罷
行幾無遺憾浹月之間所以大慰斯民之望益
光繼述之猷者至矣盡矣然猶不以聖知自居
雖在諒陰之中而不廢求賢之典首進臣等于
廷宣示
制策咨諏治道此尤足以見帝王之高致知為治
之先務也臣仰惟

〔臣〕彭數
〔臣〕對〔臣〕聞大學有曰自天子以至於庶人壹是

中格物致知誠意正心皆所用以脩其身者而

也大哉身乎體斯道而行萬化其在此乎故曾

則曰脩其身而天下平然則聖賢道學相傳曷

出於脩身之外者哉恭惟

皇上出震繼離嗣大歷服龍飛虎變御極當天聖作
神興萬物咸覩舜承堯志首行四罪之誅武纘

凡天下之所欲而未興所病而未除者以次罷
行幾無遺憾浹月之間所以大慰斯民之望益
光繼述之猷者至矣盡矣然猶不以聖知自居
雖在諒陰之中而不廢求賢之典首進〔臣〕等于
廷宣示
制策咨諏治道此先足以見帝王之高敷知爲治
之先務也〔臣〕仰惟
punctuated:
彭教。
臣對：臣聞《大學》有曰：「自天子以至於庶人，壹是皆以脩身為本。」蓋《大學》條目有八，而脩身居其中。格物、致知、誠意、正心，皆所以脩其身者；而齊家、治國、平天下，非本之脩身，則無以成其功也。大哉身乎！體斯道而行萬化，其在此乎！故曾子一傳而子思則曰：「脩身則道立。」再傳而孟子則曰：「脩其身而天下平。」然則聖賢道學相傳，固莫切於脩身，而帝王治國平天下之道，抑豈有出於脩身之外者哉？恭惟皇上出震繼離，嗣大歷服，龍飛虎變，御極當天，聖作神興，萬物咸覩。舜承堯志，首行四罪之投；武纘文謨，益隆周、召之任。屏耳目之玩，弛不急之營，凡天下之所欲而未興、所病而未除者，以次罷行，幾無遺憾。浹月之間，所以大慰斯民之望、益光繼述之猷者，至矣，盡矣！然猶不以聖知自居，雖在諒陰之中，而不廢求賢之典，首進臣等于廷，宣示制策，咨諏治道，此尤足以見帝王之高致，知為治之先務也。臣仰惟
translation_en:
Peng Jiao 彭教.

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that the Great Learning (Daxue) says: "From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all must consider the cultivation of the person as the root." Now, the Great Learning has eight specific items, and the cultivation of the person stands in their midst. Investigating things, extending knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind are all the means by which one cultivates one's person; whereas regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven cannot achieve their success unless they are rooted in the cultivation of the person. Great indeed is the person! Embodying this Way and carrying out the myriad transformations—does it not lie right here? Thus, in the first transmission from Zengzi 曾子, Zisi 子思 said: "When the person is cultivated, the Way is established." In a second transmission, Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) said: "When one's person is cultivated, all under Heaven is brought to peace." This being so, in the transmission of the Learning of the Way among sages and worthies, nothing is more essential than the cultivation of the person; and as for the Way by which emperors and kings govern the state and bring peace to all under Heaven, how could anything lie outside the cultivation of the person?

Your servant reverently reflects that Your Majesty has emerged like thunder in the trigram Zhen and succeeded to the brightness of the trigram Li, inheriting the great mandate and realm; soaring like a dragon and transforming like a tiger, You have ascended the supreme throne to match Heaven; as a sage arises and a spirit stirs, the myriad things all behold You. Like Shun 舜 carrying on the will of Yao 堯, You first carried out the banishment of the four criminals; like King Wu 武王 continuing the plans of King Wen 文王, You have further exalted the responsibilities entrusted to the Duke of Zhou 周公 and the Duke of Shao 召公. You have put aside delights of the ear and eye and relaxed non-urgent construction projects; everything that all under Heaven desires but had not yet been promoted, and everything from which it suffers but had not yet been removed, You have successively abolished or enacted, leaving almost nothing to be regretted. Within the space of a full month, that by which You have greatly comforted the hopes of the people and further glorified the plans of filial succession and continuation has reached the utmost perfection and completeness! Yet You still do not presume upon Your own sage wisdom; though in the midst of the mourning period, You have not neglected the institution of seeking out the worthy. First advancing Your servants to the court, You proclaimed the Emperor's policy question (zhice) to inquire into the Way of governance. This is especially sufficient to show the lofty attainment of an emperor and king, knowing what is the foremost task in governing. Your servant admiringly reflects that…

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
陛下毓德春宮蓋有年矣其深仁厚澤□於天下□
美主善協一得于講學之功而存心出治之要
機制治保邦之統紀得于
先帝心傳之妙一旦尊居
宸極舉而措之若建瓴然豈臣昧陋所能有裨於
聖明之萬一哉然敢不陳其狂愚以塞
明詔臣竊惟治國平天下之道有本焉有要焉本
者何脩身是也要者何用賢才正風俗是也有
其本而無其要則治道不可以徒成有其要而
無其本則治功不可以苟就是豈治國平天下
===
之道哉臣請循其本舉其要徵諸往古為
陛下陳之以信治平之說夫賢才者致治之具故曰
為國無以為寶惟善以為寶言有國之務莫要
於此也古之聖王恭已無為於上而任賢分理
於下舜之舉相命官夏之籲俊尊帝成湯任伊
尹而功格于天高宗得傅說而殷邦嘉靖文武
之興爽邦由哲為周之楨者皆棫樸卷阿之士
弼成丕基者皆義德容德之人當是之時庶政
惟和萬國咸寧下逮漢唐宋之君亦皆選任□
才以為輔佐高祖開基蕭曹為冠孝宣中興□□

punctuated: 陛下毓德春宮，蓋有年矣。其深仁厚澤□於天下，□美主善協一，得于講學之功；而存心出治之要機，制治保邦之統紀，得于先帝心傳之妙。一旦尊居宸極，舉而措之，若建瓴然。豈臣昧陋所能有裨於聖明之萬一哉？然敢不陳其狂愚，以塞明詔。臣竊惟治國平天下之道，有本焉，有要焉。本者何？脩身是也。要者何？用賢才、正風俗是也。有其本而無其要，則治道不可以徒成；有其要而無其本，則治功不可以苟就。是豈治國平天下之道哉？臣請循其本、舉其要，徵諸往古，為陛下陳之，以信治平之說。夫賢才者，致治之具。故曰：「為國無以為寶，惟善以為寶。」言有國之務，莫要於此也。古之聖王，恭已無為於上，而任賢分理於下。舜之舉相命官，夏之籲俊尊帝，成湯任伊尹而功格于天，高宗得傅說而殷邦嘉靖。文、武之興，爽邦由哲。為周之楨者，皆棫樸、卷阿之士；弼成丕基者，皆義德、容德之人。當是之時，庶政惟和，萬國咸寧。下逮漢、唐、宋之君，亦皆選任□才以為輔佐。高祖開基，蕭、曹為冠；孝宣中興，□□
translation_en: … Your Majesty nurtured Your virtue in the Eastern Palace as Heir Apparent for many years. Your deep benevolence and generous grace [?] throughout the realm, and Your [?] excellence in taking goodness as master and harmonizing in unity were gained from the effort of studying and lecturing; meanwhile, the essential pivot of preserving the mind and issuing governance, and the overarching threads of regulating rule and safeguarding the state, were gained from the subtlety of the Late Emperor's mind-to-mind transmission. Once You ascended the imperial throne, You raised and implemented them as effortlessly as pouring water from a rooftop pitcher. How could someone as ignorant and crude as Your servant possibly contribute even one ten-thousandth to Your sagely brilliance? Yet how dare I not set forth my rash foolishness to fulfill Your illustrious decree? Your servant humbly reflects that the Way of governing the state and bringing peace to the world has its root and its essentials. What is the root? It is cultivating the self. What are the essentials? They are employing worthy talents and rectifying customs and morals. If one has the root without the essentials, the Way of governance cannot be accomplished in vain; if one has the essentials without the root, the achievements of governance cannot be carelessly realized. How could that be the Way of governing the state and bringing peace to the world? Your servant begs to follow this root and raise these essentials, verifying them against antiquity, and set them forth for Your Majesty so as to substantiate the doctrine of governance and peace. Now, worthy talents are the instruments for bringing about good governance. Thus it is said: "A state does not take material wealth as its treasure; it takes only the good as its treasure." This means that among the affairs of holding a state, nothing is more essential than this. The sagely kings of antiquity maintained reverent self-restraint and non-action above, while employing the worthy to divide administrative duties below. Shun raised up ministers and appointed officials; the Xia called upon men of eminence to honor God on High; Tang the Successful employed Yi Yin and his achievements reached to Heaven; Gaozong obtained Fu Yue and the Yin state was brought to admirable tranquility. In the rise of Kings Wen and Wu, they enlightened the state through men of wisdom. Those who served as the pillars of Zhou were all gentlemen celebrated in the odes "Yupu" and "Juan'e"; those who assisted in completing the great foundation were all men of righteous virtue and tolerant virtue. At that time, the myriad administrations were harmonious and all the states were at peace. Coming down to the rulers of Han, Tang, and Song, they too all selected and employed [worthy] talents to serve as their辅佐 (aides and assistants). When Gaozu of Han founded the dynasty, Xiao He and Cao Can stood at the forefront; in the restoration under Emperor Xiaoxuan, [Bing Ji and]…

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
魏有聲房杜致太平之功姚宋成開元之治韓
范富歐用於宋而慶曆元祐之治後世稱之豈
不足以興王而躋盛治亦皆能隨世以就功名
蓋賢才之有益於人國也如此然取人為政必
本於脩道之仁則所以用賢才者豈脩身未至
者之所能辦哉至於風俗者厲世之規故曰君
子不出家而成教於國言風教之行無為而化
也先王之盛禮義之澤漸摩浸灌使民興行百
姓昭明而刑措不用遷善敏德而比屋可封虞
芮之人感禮讓之風江漢游女有士君子之行
===
民俗洽時雍之化兆民有阜成之美而三代之
隆卓乎不可及已自德色誶語之俗興而秦以
以顛自虛浮放曠之習盛而晉俗日壞東漢尚
名節之風而士之激揚風流者猶足以維持乎
世道有宋敦忠厚之習而士之正色立朝者亦
足增重於國勢風俗係治道之汙隆蓋如此主
允升大猷必由於敬典之德則所以正風俗者
亦豈聲音笑貌之所能為哉惟其為治者不知
用賢之為要而致意於用賢者又未必□□□
身是以或立賢而不能舉或舉之而不能□□

不足以興王而躋盛治亦皆能隨世以就功名
蓋賢才之有益於人國也如此然取人為政必
本於脩道之仁則所以用賢才者豈脩身未至
者之所能辦哉至於風俗者厲世之規故曰君
子不出家而成教於國言風教之行無為而化
也先王之盛禮義之澤漸摩浸灌使民與行百
姓昭明而刑措不用遷善敏德而比屋可封虞
芮之人感禮讓之風江漢游女有士君子之行
===
民俗洽時雍之化兆民有阜成之美而三代之
隆卓乎不可及已自德色誶語之俗興而嬴秦
以趨自虛浮放曠之習盛而晉俗日壞東漢尚

□是以求元賢而不能□□□之□□□□
punctuated:
魏有聲；房、杜致太平之功，姚、宋成開元之治；韓、范、富、歐用於宋，而慶曆、元祐之治，後世稱之。豈不足以興王而躋盛治，亦皆能隨世以就功名。蓋賢才之有益於人國也如此。然取人為政，必本於脩道之仁，則所以用賢才者，豈脩身未至者之所能辦哉！
至於風俗者，厲世之規，故曰：「君子不出家而成教於國。」言風教之行，無為而化也。先王之盛，禮義之澤漸摩浸灌，使民興行。百姓昭明而刑措不用，遷善敏德而比屋可封。虞、芮之人，感禮讓之風；江、漢游女，有士君子之行。民俗洽時雍之化，兆民有阜成之美，而三代之隆，卓乎不可及已。自德色誶語之俗興，而秦以以顛；自虛浮放曠之習盛，而晉俗日壞。東漢尚名節之風，而士之激揚風流者，猶足以維持乎世道；有宋敦忠厚之習，而士之正色立朝者，亦足增重於國勢。風俗係治道之汙隆，蓋如此。主允升大猷，必由於敬典之德，則所以正風俗者，亦豈聲音笑貌之所能為哉！

translation_en:
…and Wei Xiang 魏相 were renowned; Fang Xuanling 房玄齡 and Du Ruhui 杜如晦 achieved the功 merit of Great Peace, while Yao Chong 姚崇 and Song Jing 宋璟 brought about the orderly rule of the Kaiyuan 開元 era; Han Qi 韓琦, Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹, Fu Bi 富弼, and Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修 were employed under the Song, and the orderly rule of the Qingli 慶曆 and Yuanyou 元祐 eras was praised by later generations. Even if they were not quite sufficient to raise up true kingship and ascend to the pinnacle of flourishing governance, they were all nonetheless able to adapt to their times and accomplish meritorious deeds and fame. Such is the benefit that worthy talents bring to a state! Yet governing through the selection of men must be rooted in the benevolence by which one cultivates the Way; how, then, could the employment of worthy talents be managed by someone whose self-cultivation is not yet complete?

As for customs and mores, they are the standard for inspiring the age. Thus it is said: "The gentleman, without going beyond his family, brings teaching to completion throughout the state." This means that when moral influence and instruction are put into practice, transformation occurs without coercive action. At the height of the former kings' rule, the grace of rites and righteousness gradually moulded and steeped the people, causing them to rise up in moral conduct. The hundred surnames were bright and clear, so punishments were set aside and not used; they moved toward goodness and were diligent in virtue, so that every household side by side was worthy of enfeoffment. The men of Yu 虞 and Rui 芮 were moved by the ethos of courteous yielding; the wandering maidens of the Jiang 江 and Han 漢 rivers possessed the conduct of scholarly gentlemen. Popular customs were imbued with the transformation of harmonious times, the multitudinous people enjoyed the beauty of abundant fulfilment, and the splendour of the Three Dynasties stood towering beyond reach! Once the custom of wearing self-satisfied expressions over small kindnesses and trading abusive words arose, Qin 秦 thereby toppled; once the habit of hollowness, superficiality, and unrestrained licence flourished, the customs of Jin 晉 deteriorated day by day. The Eastern Han esteemed an ethos of reputation and integrity, and scholars who stirred and uplifted the moral current were still able to sustain the way of the world; the Song dynasty cultivated habits of loyalty and generosity, and scholars who stood at court with stern rectitude were likewise sufficient to add weight to the strength of the state. Such is the manner in which customs and mores are tied to the decline or flourishing of governance! Yet truly ascending to the great plan [?] must proceed from the virtue of revering the canons; how, then, could the rectification of customs be accomplished merely through the tones of one's voice and a smiling countenance?

Only because those who govern do not understand that employing the worthy is essential, and those who do turn their attention to employing the worthy do not necessarily [… cultivate their own] persons—therefore, some recognize the worthy yet cannot promote them, or promote them yet cannot […]. …

者盤據窟穴而不可搖正直剛明者遠引高蹈
而不樂於用否泰消長而國空虛乃徒惴惴於
兆民之未殖四方之未靖其亦不思之甚矣則
臣之所謂其要在用賢才者固非徒然也惟其
論治者不知風俗之為要而留心於風俗者又
未必本於脩身是以朝廷之上是非不白刑賞
不分士夫之間志趣卑污廉恥廢壞正言端色
者群譏眾排而目之為矯激阿諛軟熟者逢迎
請謁而稱之為變通天下之人靡然不知名節
===

者，好人之所惡，而惡人之所好。於是卑瑣齷齪者盤據窟穴而不可搖，正直剛明者遠引高蹈而不樂於用。否泰消長而國空虛，乃徒惴惴於兆民之未殖、四方之未靖，其亦不思之甚矣！則臣之所謂「其要在用賢才」者，固非徒然也。惟其論治者不知風俗之為要，而留心於風俗者又未必本於脩身，是以朝廷之上是非不白、刑賞不分，士夫之間志趣卑污、廉恥廢壞。正言端色者，群譏眾排，而目之為矯激；阿諛軟熟者，逢迎請謁，而稱之為變通。天下之人靡然不知名節行檢之為重，而天下之事亦將支離潰敗而不可以復為，乃徒區區於禁防之未密、法制之未周，吁，亦末矣！則臣之所謂「其要在正風俗」者，亦非苟然也。
陛下之孜孜於賢才，切矣！首降溫綸，即開薦舉之門，復精選任之政，黎獻共臣，遠邇丕應。然明揚之選，或未叶於疇咨；周行之間，尚不稱於任使。殆未足以上當陛下寤寐英豪之心也。臣願陛下脩身以任賢才，即所謂「惟仁者能愛人，能惡人」，
translation_en:
… love what others hate and hate what others love. Consequently, base, petty, and sordid men entrench themselves in their dens and cannot be dislodged, while upright, firm, and clear-sighted men withdraw far away in lofty retirement and take no pleasure in being employed. As adversity and prosperity wax and wane and the state becomes hollowed out, to then merely fret anxiously that the multitude of people have not yet prospered and the four quarters are not yet pacified—this is truly a case of extreme thoughtlessness! Thus, what your servant meant by saying that "the essential point lies in employing worthy talents" is certainly not without basis.

Because those who discuss governance do not understand that customs and morals are essential, and those who do pay attention to customs and morals do not necessarily root them in self-cultivation, right and wrong are not made clear and punishments and rewards are not properly distinguished in the court above, while among the scholar-officials, aspirations become base and corrupt and the sense of honor and shame is ruined and abandoned. Those who speak uprightly and maintain a proper countenance are mocked by the crowd and pushed out by the multitude, who label them as affectedly extreme; those who flatter and are slickly compliant curry favor and seek private audiences, and are praised as adaptable. People throughout the realm are swept along, no longer knowing the importance of moral integrity and personal conduct, and the affairs of the realm are about to become fragmented, collapsing beyond the point where anything can be done about them. To then busy oneself merely with the fact that prohibitions and safeguards are not yet tight enough or that laws and regulations are not yet comprehensive—alas, that is merely attending to the branches! Thus, what your servant meant by saying that "the essential point lies in rectifying customs and morals" is also not said lightly.

Your Majesty's assiduous pursuit of worthy talents is earnest indeed! Having first sent down gracious decrees, You immediately opened the gate of recommendation and promotion and further refined the administration of selection and appointment; the eminent worthies among the multitude have together become Your subjects, and near and far have grandly responded. Yet those selected for open promotion perhaps do not yet accord with Your inquiries and consultations, and among those in the ranks of office, some still do not measure up to their appointments and commissions. This is scarcely enough to match on high Your Majesty's heart, which longs waking and sleeping for heroes and men of distinction. title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
有克知灼見之明有迪知忱恂之哲則賢能之
進如茅斯拔而不致於跋胡疐前却之患庸邪之
退如距斯脫而無所幸於姑息容養之私然後
翕受敷施隨材器使大者贊元經體以亮天工
細者居官任職以熈庶績能外事者任典戎榦
方之責明治體者備拾遺補過之官布列中外
之間以共圖天下之事則天下國家之治可得
而成矣
陛下之汲汲於風俗至矣重奔競之罰杜倖進之途
長寛厚之風除苛刻之政天下亹亹嚮風承德
===
然君子未能於有耻小人未盡於革心或未足
以仰酬
陛下敦大成裕之意也臣願
陛下脩身以正風俗即所謂堯舜帥天下以仁而民
從之其好惡之端既足以示人之趋嚮而真實
之意又有以孚人於觀感風俗既成人知所尚
將見知耻好義不必爵賞刑罰一一加其身而
後有所勸戒不待勸勉程督人人致其敬而後
有所脩飭興仁興讓之俗臻敎成於國之效著
則天下國家之治可得而久矣夫用賢才以成

punctuated:
有克知灼見之明，有迪知忱恂之哲，則賢能之進如茅斯拔，而不致於跋胡疐前却之患；庸邪之退如距斯脫，而無所幸於姑息容養之私。然後翕受敷施，隨材器使：大者贊元經體，以亮天工；細者居官任職，以熈庶績；能外事者任典戎榦方之責；明治體者備拾遺補過之官。布列中外之間，以共圖天下之事，則天下國家之治可得而成矣。
陛下之汲汲於風俗至矣。重奔競之罰，杜倖進之途，長寛厚之風，除苛刻之政，天下亹亹嚮風承德。然君子未能於有耻，小人未盡於革心，或未足以仰酬陛下敦大成裕之意也。臣願陛下脩身以正風俗，即所謂「堯舜帥天下以仁而民從之」。其好惡之端既足以示人之趋嚮，而真實之意又有以孚人於觀感。風俗既成，人知所尚，將見知耻好義，不必爵賞刑罰一一加其身而後有所勸戒；不待勸勉程督，人人致其敬而後有所脩飭。興仁興讓之俗臻，敎成於國之效著，則天下國家之治可得而久矣。夫用賢才以成

…possessing the discernment of thorough knowledge and clear perception, and the wisdom of enlightened understanding and sincere trustworthiness—then the advancement of the worthy and capable will be like pulling up cogon grass by the roots, without suffering the dilemma of stepping on the wolf's dewlap or tripping on its tail [hesitating to advance or retreat]; and the dismissal of the mediocre and wicked will be like casting off spurs, leaving them no chance to profit from the partiality of indulgent toleration. Thereafter, gather and accept them all and widely employ them, assigning offices according to their talents: the great ones assisting in prime governance and ordering the state structure, so as to aid the work of Heaven; the lesser ones holding offices and fulfilling duties, so as to make all achievements flourish; those capable in external affairs taking on the responsibilities of commanding the military and defending the regions; and those who understand the principles of governance filling the offices of remonstrating against omissions and rectifying faults. Arrayed throughout the court and the provinces to jointly plan the affairs of the Empire, the good governance of the Empire and the state can thereby be accomplished!

Your Majesty's earnestness regarding customs and morals has reached the utmost! You have increased the penalties for opportunistic self-seeking, blocked the paths of unmerited advancement, fostered a climate of generosity and magnanimity, and abolished harsh and severe policies, so that the Empire tirelessly turns toward your influence and receives your virtue. Yet gentlemen are not yet able to have a true sense of shame, and petty men have not completely reformed their hearts; perhaps this is not yet sufficient to look up and repay Your Majesty's intention of cultivating greatness and achieving abundance. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would cultivate Your person in order to rectify customs and morals—which is what is meant by "Yao and Shun led the Empire with benevolence and the people followed them." Once the manifestations of Your likes and dislikes are sufficient to show people the direction to pursue, Your genuine intentions will moreover inspire trust in people through what they observe and feel. When customs that promote benevolence and humility are reached, and the effect of teaching accomplished throughout the state becomes manifest, then the good governance of the Empire and the state can be made enduring! title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
治功於一時正風俗以綱維治道於終久隆平
之道誠莫要於此矣而一身玄養德身修政身
也者萬化之原萬事之幹其所以為取人之則
教化之端胥此焉出所謂身脩而後家齊家齊
而後國治國治而後天下平者以此
陛下知一身繫於天下國家其重如此而不敢以少
忽焉必使言有則而行有常以立大中而守至
正則推之於國達之天下以之用賢才以之正
風俗治具畢舉德化風行邁迹往古增光
先烈將唯
===
陛下之所為無不如志矣若夫政事之失得民生之
利病因革之所宜脩攘之所切固臣之所欲縷
指而條陳諒亦
陛下之所樂聞而嘉納者然臣竊以為不急其要而
泛及其他不本於
陛下之身而營營馳騁於事為功利之末則非所以
端出治之本清應物之源正宏綱大紀之所在
其何以贊
陛下宏遠之圖惟新之治哉故臣冒昧輒陳其說如
此而懇懇焉以脩身為勸也雖然身者家國之

punctuated: 治功於一時，正風俗以綱維治道於終久，隆平之道，誠莫要於此矣。而一身玄養德身修政，身也者，萬化之原、萬事之幹，其所以為取人之則、教化之端，胥此焉出。所謂「身脩而後家齊，家齊而後國治，國治而後天下平」者，以此。陛下知一身繫於天下國家，其重如此，而不敢以少忽焉，必使言有則而行有常，以立大中而守至正，則推之於國，達之天下，以之用賢才，以之正風俗，治具畢舉，德化風行，邁迹往古，增光先烈，將唯陛下之所為，無不如志矣。若夫政事之失得、民生之利病、因革之所宜、脩攘之所切，固臣之所欲縷指而條陳，諒亦陛下之所樂聞而嘉納者。然臣竊以為不急其要而泛及其他，不本於陛下之身而營營馳騁於事為功利之末，則非所以端出治之本、清應物之源、正宏綱大紀之所在，其何以贊陛下宏遠之圖、惟新之治哉？故臣冒昧輒陳其說如此，而懇懇焉以脩身為勸也。雖然，身者家國之
translation_en: … achievements of governance for the moment, and rectifying customs in order to uphold the way of governance for the long term—in the way of prosperous peace, truly nothing is more essential than this. Yet one's own person is where virtue is cultivated and governance is ordered [?]. The person is the source of all transformations and the trunk of all affairs; that which serves as the standard for selecting men and the beginning of moral transformation all issues forth from this. What is meant by "when the person is cultivated, the family is regulated; when the family is regulated, the state is rightly governed; when the state is rightly governed, the world is made tranquil" is on account of this. If Your Majesty knows that Your single person is bound up with the empire and the state, that its weight is such as this, and dares not neglect it in the slightest—ensuring that words have rules and actions have constancy, so as to establish the Great Mean and hold fast to the Utmost Correctness—then when extended to the state and carried throughout the empire, using this to employ worthy talents and using this to rectify customs, the instruments of governance will all be raised up, moral transformation will sweep like the wind, surpassing the traces of antiquity and adding luster to the achievements of Your predecessors; then whatever Your Majesty does, nothing will fail to accord with Your will. As for the successes and failures of administrative affairs, the benefits and ills of the people's livelihood, what is appropriate in continuity and change, and what is urgent in internal cultivation and external defense—these are indeed what Your servant wishes to point out in detail and set forth item by item, and I trust they are also what Your Majesty would gladly hear and approvingly accept. Yet Your servant privately considers that if one does not press upon what is essential, but instead ranges broadly over other matters; if one does not root it in Your Majesty's own person, but busily gallops after the branches of practical deeds and utilitarian profit, then this is not the way to rectify the root from which governance issues, to clear the source of responding to things, or to establish where the great guiding principles and major norms reside. How then could it assist Your Majesty's far-reaching plans and newly inaugurated governance? Therefore Your servant has presumptuously set forth his views like this, and earnestly urges the cultivation of the person. Even so, the person is the [root] of family, state, [and empire]…

translation_en: … the Empire, and the mind, in turn, is the master of the person. Therefore, those who served their sovereigns in antiquity made rectifying the ruler's mind their sole priority, for they too understood this principle. Now, a single mind is subtle and minute, yet the things that assail it are legion—all the more so when one occupies the position of supreme veneration and wields power by which nothing is unattainable! Thus, sounds and sights, aromas and flavors, roaming at leisure and galloping in the hunt, the splendor of building projects and the accumulation of wealth and profit—all these crowd forward together in motley array, growing newer by the day and more abundant by the month. Meanwhile, sycophantic favorites in one's entourage who artfully watch for openings to cater to the ruler's whims and fancies are of many kinds. Although Your Majesty possesses lofty and brilliant sagely insight and a firm and steadfast sacred will, and will surely neither be shaken by external things and affairs nor be blinded and deluded by petty, self-serving men, how could You not pay special heed to the means of aiding the nourishment and moral cultivation of this mind, and of maintaining the defenses of restraint and admonition? The great Song-dynasty Confucian scholar Cheng Yi 程頤 once submitted counsel to his sovereign, saying: "If during a single day a ruler spends the greater part of his time receiving worthy scholar-officials, he can thereby nourish his temperament and mold his moral nature." At the time this was regarded as a celebrated maxim, and later generations have praised it as the ultimate discourse. Now, as Your Majesty is at the very beginning of putting governmental instruction into practice—truly the moment for bestowing upon Yourself a wise mandate—You should gaze afar with transcendent vision and ponder deeply the supreme plan. Mindful of what the sovereign's virtue depends upon and attentive to how environment and habit transform and nourish one's disposition, You should carefully select literary and scholarly officials, choosing gentlemen who are prudent, sincere, pure, and admirable, upright, steadfast, and outspoken. Have them attend the imperial cortege and keep roster duty in the palace lodges, to fill the ranks of Expositors-in-waiting and Readers-in-waiting and to serve during Your Majesty's moments of serene leisure. After holding court, repair at once to the side halls to receive and consult them at ease, discussing the Way of governance so that they may enlighten and enrich Your mind as occasion arises and offer admonition and remonstrance in response to matters at hand; even down to the feelings of the people, the conditions of the world, and the hardships of sowing and reaping, all may be fully set forth before Your presence. Yet the reality of reading books and embodying the Way lies especially…

punctuated: 要於經，治亂安危之迹莫備於史。宜令各專其說，分日進講，不限常式，而得悉意以開陳；無所避忌，而得隨事為勸戒。至於《祖訓條章》、《三朝寳訓》，祖宗之成憲斯在，國家之令典具存，常經聽覽，庶習舊章。則朝夕與居者莫匪正人，洋溢聽聞者無非善道。聖心湛然而無蔽，聖德純一而不雜，于以坐九重，員斧扆，南面而聽斷，紹列聖之宏撫，垂萬世之永聞，豈不休哉！臣草茅微賤，學術庸疎，蒙國家之教養，承陛下之登進，輒以所學妄有陳論。伏望留神省覽，涓埃之微，或有增於海嶽，則足以彰陛下策士求言之實意，而臣亦不為闊迂無用之虛言矣。若夫阿志逢迎，有所規避，以徼一命之寵，陛下亦將焉用之哉！干犯天威，無任戰慄恐懼之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …essential in the Classics, and the traces of order and disorder, security and danger, are nowhere more complete than in the Histories. It is fitting to command each of them to specialize in his own exposition and take turns presenting lectures on different days, not bound by routine formulas so that they may fully express their thoughts in setting forth their views, and free from taboos or evasions so that they may offer encouragement and admonition as matters arise. As for the Articles of the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun tiaozhang) and the Precious Injunctions of the Three Reigns (Sanchao baoxun), wherein lie the established constitutions of the imperial ancestors and wherein the fine statutes of the state are preserved in their entirety, if Your Majesty regularly hears and peruses them, you will become thoroughly familiar with the old canons. Then those who dwell with you morning and evening will all be upright men, and what fills your hearing will all be the way of goodness. Your sacred mind will be limpid and unclouded; your sacred virtue will be pure, unified, and unmixed. Thereby seated within the Ninefold Palace, with your back [員, for 負] to the axe-embroidered screen, facing south to hear and decide affairs of state, you will carry on the grand rule [撫, for 模?] of the successive sage-emperors and hand down an enduring reputation for ten thousand generations—would this not be glorious! Your servant is of humble, rustic origins, and my scholarship is mediocre and superficial. Having received the education and nurturing of the state and been favored with promotion by Your Majesty, I have presumed to draw upon what I have learned to rashly set forth my arguments. Humbly I hope that you will deign to fix your attention and examine them. Should a tiny trickle or grain of dust perhaps add something to the seas and mountains, it will suffice to manifest Your Majesty's sincere intention in examining scholars by policy questions to seek their counsel, and my words too will not have been pedantic, impractical, and useless empty talk. As for flattering your wishes and currying favor, or evading issues in order to angle for the grace of a first official appointment—what use would Your Majesty have for such a man! Having offended the Heavenly Majesty, I am overcome with the utmost trembling and fear. Your servant respectfully replies.

translation_en: Your servant respectfully replies: Your servant has heard it said in the Classic [the Great Learning (Daxue)]: "The ancients who wished to manifest luminous virtue throughout the world first governed their states; wishing to govern their states, they first regulated their families; wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons; wishing to cultivate their persons, they first rectified their minds; wishing to rectify their minds, they first made their intentions sincere; wishing to make their intentions sincere, they first extended their knowledge; and the extension of knowledge lay in the investigation of things." How supreme are the words of the sages of antiquity! Their phrasing is concise, their meaning broad, and their principle profound; their sequence is like spring, summer, autumn, and winter, which cannot be thrown into disorder; their utility is like grain, millet, cloth, and silk, which cannot be dispensed with. No person may neglect them, and for the ruler of men they are especially urgent. Since childhood, your servant has recited and pondered this Classic by day, and studied and savored it by night, believing that if the ruler of men in governing the world sets this aside and seeks elsewhere, it is like whipping a worn-out horse down a dark road without Wang Liang 王良 or Zao Fu 造父 to guide it from before and behind—to wish to reach the Great Way thus, is it not difficult indeed! How might I once set this forth before my Sovereign, so as to make my Sovereign a ruler like Yao 堯 and Shun 舜, and make this age an age like that of Yao and Shun! Your servant has cherished this aspiration for a long time, fearing only that I would grow old in mountain caves with no means of presenting myself. Now I have obtained the opportunity to stand in the Great Court and receive Your Majesty's inquiry, in which not a word touches upon matters of cloth and silk, money and grain, military forces, or penal administration, whereas words on governing the state and bringing peace to the world shine as brightly as the sun and stars. Your servant bowed twice and knocked his head to the ground, holding the question in both hands and reciting it, feeling as though a chronic illness had been broken and a heavy burden lifted, so that the thoughts I have long cherished can be poured forth all at once—how exhilarating it is! Humbly reading…

〔策〕書有曰朕惟臨軒策士乃我
祖宗法古求治之盛典也茲朕兢兢在疚事雖不敢
妨廢而情有不能安然行之者顧爾多士游心經
史於治國平天下之道講之熟矣朕雖不臨軒詳
問爾多士其各敷陳所蘊以獻〔臣臣〕惟兢兢在疚者
陛下之仁孝也〔臣臣〕知
陛下處此諒陰之中思慕哀痛之切無以加矣而不
敢妨廢者遵
祖宗之舊典也必以治國平天下為言者自其所急
者言也亦不棄於草茅之賤也夫舊典固所當
===
遵而〔臣臣〕言亦當見用〔臣臣〕恐
陛下以為應故事而已雖然
陛下以故事策〔臣臣〕不敢以故事應也恭聞
陛下昔在東宮仁孝之聲無遠不諭比來嗣登
太寶垂衣御極
明詔一下遠近帖服至有垂涕泣而感戴者是何其
仁之入人深也及聞虎豹犀犬鷹隼之屬不□
於用者悉令屏去又何其見之明也即是而
則
陛下求言將以有為非特應故事而已〔臣臣〕敢□□
punctuated: □策有曰：「朕惟臨軒策士，乃我祖宗法古求治之盛典也。茲朕煢煢在疚，事雖不欲妨廢，而情有不能安然行之者。顧尔多士，游心經史，於治國平天下之道，講之熟矣。朕雖不臨軒詳問，爾多士其各敷陳所蘊以獻。」臣惟「煢煢在疚」者，陛下之仁孝也。臣知陛下處此諒陰之中，思慕哀痛之切，無以加矣。而不敢妨廢者，遵祖宗之舊典也；必以治國平天下為言者，自其所急者言也，亦不棄於草茅之賤也。夫舊典固所當遵，而臣言亦當見用，臣恐陛下以為應故事而已。雖然，陛下以故事策臣，臣不敢以故事應也。恭聞陛下昔在東宮，仁孝之聲，無遠不諭。比来嗣登太寶，垂衣御極，明詔一下，遠近帖服，至有垂涕泣而感戴者，是何其仁之入人深也！及聞虎豹犀犬鷹隼之属，不切於用者，悉令屏去，又何其見之明也！即是而□，則陛下求言，將以有為，非特應故事而已。臣敢不竭□
translation_en:
… the [Imperial] policy question, which states: “We reflect that appearing at the palace verandah to put policy questions to scholars is the grand ceremony whereby Our Imperial Ancestors modeled themselves on antiquity and sought good governance. Now, as We stand solitary and grieving in mourning, although We do not wish this affair to be impeded or neglected, in Our feelings We cannot carry it out with an easy heart. Considering that all you scholars have immersed your minds in the Classics and Histories, you have thoroughly discussed the Way of governing the state and bringing peace to the world. Even though We do not appear at the palace verandah to question you in detail, let each of you scholars set forth in full the learning you have accumulated and present it.”

Your servant reflects that “standing solitary and grieving in mourning” is the benevolent filiality of Your Majesty. Your servant knows that as Your Majesty abides in this period of imperial mourning, the earnestness of Your yearning and grief could not be surpassed. Yet that You dare not let this affair be impeded or neglected is to follow the established institutions of the Imperial Ancestors; and that You necessarily speak of governing the state and bringing peace to the world is to speak from what is most urgent, and also not to spurn the humble among the rustics. Now, the established institutions ought certainly to be followed, and your servant's words ought also to be put to use; yet your servant fears that Your Majesty may regard this merely as fulfilling a routine formality. Even so, if Your Majesty puts policy questions to your servant as a routine formality, your servant would not dare to respond merely as a routine formality.

Your servant has reverently heard that when Your Majesty was formerly in the Eastern Palace [as Heir Apparent], the renown of Your benevolent filiality was known to the farthest reaches. Recently, upon succeeding to the Great Treasure [the throne] and governing from the supreme seat with robes hanging down, as soon as Your enlightened edict was handed down, those far and near submitted in peace, to the point that some shed tears in gratitude and devotion—how deeply Your benevolence has entered into the hearts of the people! And when your servant heard that tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, hounds, falcons, and hawks, and creatures of that sort which are of no practical use, were all ordered to be cast away—how brilliant is Your insight! [Judging] from this, Your Majesty's seeking of counsel is with the intention of accomplishing great things, and not merely to fulfill a routine formality. How could your servant dare not exhaust his [sincerity] …

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
以對所願於
陛下者虛己聽之而已易曰君子以虛受人書曰惟
學遜志夫以匹夫之賤而瀆
萬乘之尊苟非虛心遜志則臣言何自而入乎粵觀
天生斯民强弱善惡之不同風移習染之各異
故天必生出類之才起而君長之治之而爭奪
息道之而生養遂敎之而倫理明若堯若舜若
禹湯文武所謂起而君長之者求其當時致治
之道一以格致誠正為之本脩身齊家為之則
而典章文物則以為輔治之具不在所重也若
===
漢若唐若宋其間英君誼辟亦皆所謂起而君
長之者迹其當時致治之本曰清淨曰法術曰
智謀而格致誠正則以為迂談不在所急也其
所治之道不同而所致之效亦異故三代之時
比屋可封人人君子而漢唐之盛僅曰富庶先
儒謂治不若三代者皆苟道也則漢唐宋之於
三代正猶碔砆之於美玉小徑之於大道其純
駁險易何其遠哉今
陛下所謂治國平天下者將如三代邪抑為漢唐宋
邪漢唐宋之治六朝五代之巨擘三代之遺□

陛下所以治天下者將如三代耶抑為漢唐宋
耶漢唐宋之治六朝五代之巨擘三代無窮
punctuated:
以對。所願於陛下者，虛己聽之而已。《易》曰：「君子以虛受人。」《書》曰：「惟學遜志。」夫以匹夫之賤，而瀆萬乘之尊，苟非虛心遜志，則臣言何自而入乎？

粵觀天生斯民，强弱善惡之不同，風移習染之各異，故天必生出類之才，起而君長之。治之而爭奪息，道之而生養遂，敎之而倫理明。若堯、若舜、若禹、湯、文、武，所謂起而君長之者，求其當時致治之道，一以格、致、誠、正為之本，脩身、齊家為之則，而典章文物，則以為輔治之具，不在所重也。若漢、若唐、若宋，其間英君誼辟，亦皆所謂起而君長之者，迹其當時致治之本，曰清淨、曰法術、曰智謀，而格、致、誠、正，則以為迂談，不在所急也。其所治之道不同，而所致之效亦異。故三代之時，比屋可封，人人君子；而漢、唐之盛，僅曰富庶。先儒謂：「治不若三代者，皆苟道也。」則漢、唐、宋之於三代，正猶碔砆之於美玉，小徑之於大道，其純駁險易，何其遠哉！

今陛下所謂治國平天下者，將如三代邪？抑為漢、唐、宋邪？漢、唐、宋之治，六朝、五代之巨擘，三代之遺□
translation_en:
… to reply. All that I wish of Your Majesty is that You listen with an open mind. The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "The noble man receives people with an open mind." The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "In learning, one should be humble in mind." Indeed, for a lowly commoner to importune the exalted Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots, if You are not open-minded and humble in will, how could Your servant's words ever find entry?

Looking back, when Heaven gave birth to the people, they differed in strength and weakness, goodness and evil, and varied in how they were shifted by customs and steeped in habits. Therefore, Heaven necessarily produced talents surpassing their kind to rise up and act as their rulers and leaders: governing them so that contention and seizure ceased, guiding them so that their livelihood and nourishment were fulfilled, and instructing them so that human moral relations were made clear. Such figures as Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu were those who rose up to act as rulers and leaders. If we seek the Way by which they achieved good governance in their times, they uniformly took the investigation of things, the extension of knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind as the root; they took cultivating the person and regulating the family as the standard; whereas institutions, statutes, and cultural artifacts were regarded merely as instruments to assist governance, not where the emphasis lay. As for the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, the heroic rulers and righteous sovereigns among them were also those who rose up to act as rulers and leaders. Yet if we trace the roots of how they achieved governance in their times, they spoke of quietist non-action, of legalist statecraft, and of clever stratagems; whereas the investigation of things, the extension of knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind were dismissed as pedantic talk, not among their urgent priorities. Because the Ways by which they governed were different, the results they achieved also diverged. Thus, in the time of the Three Dynasties, every household was worthy of enfeoffment and every person was a noble man; whereas at the height of the Han and Tang, it was merely called wealthy and populous. Earlier Confucians said: "Any governance that does not match the Three Dynasties follows a makeshift Way." Thus, the relation of the Han, Tang, and Song to the Three Dynasties is just like that of an inferioralabaster-like stone to fine jade, or a narrow footpath to a great thoroughfare—how vast is the distance between them in purity and impurity, danger and ease!

Now, in what Your Majesty calls governing the state and bringing peace to the world, will You emulate the Three Dynasties, or will You practice the way of the Han, Tang, and Song? The governance of the Han, Tang, and Song was the supreme model for the Six Dynasties and Five Dynasties, yet the remnant [?] of the Three Dynasties …

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
□□知
陛下所不欲為臣所素學者亦不在是臣安敢曲臺
以瀆
天威雖然欲為三代之治不可由漢唐宋之道由漢
唐宋之道而求三代之治是猶却步求前臣恐
徒走而無功也然則欲求三代之治者當何如
哉曰致知曰誠意曰正心曰脩身齊家之數者
而已
陛下必欲求三代之治則此數者之功不可缺一循
其序而行之請自致知始臣聞
===
天朝有經筵之設以為講明聖學之所臣願
陛下日御經筵選老成持重孝弟慈祥者充
經筵官進講之際必
賜之坐和顔色以待之使得盡情詳告凡天地之所
以高深鬼神之所以屈伸山海之所以流峙人
倫物理之所以當為而當行者皆如指掌焉則
陛下義理之心日明所謂治平之道如燭照而數計
蓍筮而龜卜無復有所蔽矣况日接孝弟慈祥
之人則有以鎮其躁而消其邪日改月化有不
知其所以然者而知無不至而意可誠矣誠其

translation_en:
… [?] I know that this is what Your Majesty does not wish to do, and what your servant has long studied does not lie in this either; how would your servant dare to offer compromised counsel [曲臺, for 曲學?] to profane the Heavenly Majesty! Even so, if one wishes to achieve the governance of the Three Dynasties, one cannot follow the Way of Han, Tang, and Song. To seek the governance of the Three Dynasties by following the Way of Han, Tang, and Song is like walking backward while seeking to go forward; your servant fears that it would be running in vain without achievement. If that is so, then how should one who wishes to seek the governance of the Three Dynasties proceed? It is simply a matter of these several things: extending knowledge, making the intentions sincere, rectifying the mind, cultivating the person, and regulating the family. If Your Majesty अवश्य [certainly] wishes to seek the governance of the Three Dynasties, then not one of the efforts among these several things can be lacking. To practice them by following their proper sequence, I beg that you begin with extending knowledge.

Your servant has heard that the Heavenly Court has the institution of the Classics Colloquium (jingyan), which serves as the place for expounding and illuminating the Sagely Learning. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would daily attend the Classics Colloquium, and select mature, dignified, filial, fraternal, compassionate, and benevolent men to serve as Classics Colloquium Officials. When they advance to lecture, you should always grant them seats and treat them with a gentle countenance, enabling them to explain everything thoroughly and in full detail—so that why Heaven and Earth are high and deep, why ghosts and spirits contract and expand, why mountains stand tall and seas flow, and why human relationships and the principles of things ought to be done and practiced, are all as clear as pointing to one's palm. Then Your Majesty's mind of moral principle will grow brighter by the day, and what is called the Way of governing the state and bringing peace to the world will be like illuminating with a candle and counting numbers, or divining with yarrow stalks and tortoise shells, with nothing obscured any longer. Moreover, by daily associating with filial, fraternal, compassionate, and benevolent men, there will be the means to calm restlessness and dispel perversity; changing by the day and transforming by the month without even realizing how it happens, knowledge will be extended to the utmost, and the intentions can then be made sincere. title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
意者自其心之所發者而謹之蓋心之發善惡
所由適之幾於此而善則為堯舜於此而不善
則為辛受善且偽焉則為齊桓晉文臣願
陛下惺惺自察使一念之發有善而無惡善念之生
真實而無偽惟欲足乎已而不為乎人則意無
不誠而心可正矣正其心者自其身之所主者
而謹之蓋心之應萬物預有喜焉則見者無不
喜預有怒焉則見者無不怒或有時而不存則
又如槁木死灰不相管攝
陛下之心日應萬幾若先存喜怒心則賞罰俱僭而
===
或時不存則又無以令眾庶臣願
陛下敬以直內使此心如鑑之空如衡之平喜怒之
不留忿懥之不撓有所聞必聞有所見必見則
心無不正而身可脩矣脩身所以為人之則也
親愛好惡之不偏則身脩矣
陛下位高勢尊華言華服者左右而居一有愛心則
不知其惡矣孤臣孽子遠處一方一有憎心則
不知其善矣臣願
陛下慎重噸笑無妄與人衆察忠良勿鉤賤戚則身
無不脩而家可齊矣人主之家貴賤妻妾之分

punctuated: 意者，自其心之所發者而謹之。蓋心之發，善惡所由適之幾。於此而善，則為堯、舜；於此而不善，則為辛受；善且偽焉，則為齊桓、晉文。臣願陛下惺惺自察，使一念之發，有善而無惡；善念之生，真實而無偽。惟欲足乎已，而不為乎人，則意無不誠而心可正矣。正其心者，自其身之所主者而謹之。蓋心之應萬物，預有喜焉，則見者無不喜；預有怒焉，則見者無不怒；或有時而不存，則又如槁木死灰，不相管攝。陛下之心，日應萬幾，若先存喜怒心，則賞罰俱僭；而或時不存，則又無以令眾庶。臣願陛下敬以直內，使此心如鑑之空，如衡之平，喜怒之不留，忿懥之不撓，有所聞必聞，有所見必見，則心無不正而身可脩矣。脩身，所以為人之則也。親愛好惡之不偏，則身脩矣。陛下位高勢尊，華言華服者左右而居，一有愛心，則不知其惡矣；孤臣孽子遠處一方，一有憎心，則不知其善矣。臣願陛下慎重噸笑，無妄與人；衆察忠良，勿鉤賤戚，則身無不脩而家可齊矣。人主之家，貴賤妻妾之分，
translation_en:
…thoughts is to be cautious regarding what emanates from one's mind. For the emanation of the mind is the subtle pivot from which good and evil diverge. If at this juncture it is good, one becomes a Yao or a Shun; if at this juncture it is not good, one becomes a Xin Shou [King Zhou of Shang]; if it is good yet feigned, one becomes a Duke Huan of Qi or a Duke Wen of Jin. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty remain ever alert in self-examination, ensuring that when a single thought arises, there is good and no evil, and that when a good thought is born, it is genuine and without falsity. Desiring only to find satisfaction within oneself and not acting merely for the sake of others, there will be no thought that is not sincere, and the mind can then be rectified.

To rectify one's mind is to be cautious regarding that which serves as the master of one's person. For when the mind responds to the myriad things, if it harbors pleasure beforehand, then whatever it perceives will be viewed with pleasure; if it harbors anger beforehand, then whatever it perceives will be viewed with anger; and if at times the mind is absent, it becomes like withered wood and dead ashes, exercising no control. Your Majesty's mind responds daily to a myriad of affairs; if you harbor pleasure or anger beforehand in your mind, both rewards and punishments will go awry; and if at times your mind is absent, you will have no means to command the multitude of common people. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty use reverence to straighten the interior, making this mind as empty as a mirror and as level as a balance—retaining neither pleasure nor anger, unswayed by wrath, ensuring that when there is something to hear it is truly heard, and when there is something to see it is truly seen. Then there will be no aspect of the mind that is not rectified, and the person can be cultivated.

Cultivating the person is the means to set a standard for others. When affection, fondness, liking, and disliking are free of bias, the person is cultivated. Your Majesty occupies an exalted position and commands supreme authority. Those of flowery speech and华丽 attire dwell at your side; once you harbor a feeling of fondness toward them, you will be blind to their faults. Solitary ministers and marginalized sons dwell far away in distant quarters; once you harbor a feeling of aversion toward them, you will be blind to their merits. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty be circumspect with every frown and smile [reading 噸 as 顰], never bestowing them recklessly upon others, examining the loyal and good through the judgment of the multitude, and not being ensnared by lowly relatives [?]. Then there will be no aspect of your person that is not cultivated, and the family can be regulated. As for the family of a ruler, the distinctions between noble and base, wife and concubine…

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
廷之序則廉宮室之親睦九族之親而已
陛下誠推仁以施恩義以正分使內外之間截然安
定則家無不齊而國可治矣治其國者豈必嚴
刑峻法而後治哉君仁莫不仁君義莫不義正
心誠意之外無他道也平天下者奚必挾謀用
術而後平哉上老老而民興孝上長長而民興
弟正心誠意之外無他術也夫是八者之功不
可缺一非謂了此一事而後可及彼也亦非謂
盡此一事而其餘不待致力也但其序有後先
其功有難易格致誠正在所當先而脩齊治平
===
為之後也誠意正心為難而其餘則為易也三
代行之而有餘五伯假之而不足董子言之而
止於正心韓愈推之而無曰致知格物是皆無
根之木無源之水烏能造其極哉惟宋之時雖
無真主而有真儒故朱熹將入對人告之曰方
今天子厭聞誠意正心之說子勿復言熹應之
曰某所素學者在是知而不言是欺君也臣今
亦不敢負欺君之罪而
陛下亦非厭聞誠意正心之說者故敢撫其大旨
獻臣自周至宋計有餘年上自宋迄

translation_en: …the order of the court [?], it is simply a matter of keeping upright the intimacy of the palace quarters and harmonizing the kinship of the nine degrees of relatives. If Your Majesty truly extends benevolence to bestow grace and uses righteousness to rectify distinctions of status, so that the inner and outer realms are clearly ordered and settled, then the family cannot fail to be regulated, and the state can be governed. In governing the state, why must one rely on severe punishments and harsh laws before it is governed? When the ruler is benevolent, none fail to be benevolent; when the ruler is righteous, none fail to be righteous—beyond rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere, there is no other Way. In bringing peace to the world, why must one harbor schemes and employ stratagems before it is brought to peace? When superiors treat the aged as the aged should be treated, the people are aroused to filial piety; when superiors treat elders as elders should be treated, the people are aroused to fraternal respect—beyond rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere, there is no other art. Now, not one of the efforts of these eight steps can be lacking. This does not mean that only after finishing one matter may one proceed to the next, nor does it mean that once one matter is exhausted the rest require no effort. Rather, their sequence has a before and an after, and their effort has a difficult and an easy: investigating things, extending knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind must come first, while cultivating the person, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world come after; making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind are difficult, while the rest are easy. The Three Dynasties practiced them and had more than enough; the Five Hegemons feigned them and fell short. Master Dong [Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒] spoke of them yet stopped at rectifying the mind; Han Yu 韓愈 traced them yet said nothing of extending knowledge and investigating things. These are all trees without roots and waters without a source—how could they reach the ultimate? Only in the time of the Song, though there was no true ruler, there were true Confucians. Thus, when Zhu Xi 朱熹 was about to enter for an audience, someone told him: "Nowadays the Son of Heaven is weary of hearing the doctrine of making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind; you should not speak of it again." Xi replied: "What I have always studied lies right here. To know it and not speak of it is to deceive the ruler." Today your servant likewise dares not bear the crime of deceiving the ruler, and Your Majesty is moreover not one who is weary of hearing the doctrine of making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind; therefore I dare to gather its main purport and present it. title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
幾五百年矣孟軻氏曰五百年必有王者興今
陛下應時而出其為真主邪臣拭目于茲久矣第念
陛下必不肯自列於漢唐宋之間夫既不欲列於漢
唐宋必思等乎堯舜不為堯舜非惟
陛下之心有所不足亦臣之所耻也今當何如哉曰
致知格物曰誠意正心曰脩身齊家而已所謂
治國平天下者則舉此而措之耳又豈待求之
於智謀術數之末哉今之論治國平天下者曰
足兵食曰充國用曰增戶口曰廣土地此豈為
善治平者哉傳不云乎有德此有人有人此有
===
土有土此有財有財此有用臣據所聞為
陛下獻如此雖未必切於時宜亦非迂談也倘沐
清覽則臣等幸甚天下幸甚臣不勝愛
君之至謹冒萬死以對

punctuated: 幾五百年矣。孟軻氏曰：「五百年必有王者興。」今陛下應時而出，其為真主邪？臣拭目于茲久矣。第念陛下必不肯自列於漢、唐、宋之間；夫既不欲列於漢、唐、宋，必思等乎堯、舜。不為堯、舜，非惟陛下之心有所不足，亦臣之所耻也。今當何如哉？曰致知格物，曰誠意正心，曰脩身齊家而已。所謂治國平天下者，則舉此而措之耳，又豈待求之於智謀術數之末哉！今之論治國平天下者，曰足兵食，曰充國用，曰增戶口，曰廣土地，此豈為善治平者哉？《傳》不云乎：「有德此有人，有人此有土，有土此有財，有財此有用。」臣據所聞為陛下獻如此，雖未必切於時宜，亦非迂談也。倘沐清覽，則臣等幸甚，天下幸甚。臣不勝愛君之至，謹冒萬死以對。
translation_en: …nearly five hundred years. Meng Ke 孟軻 (Mencius) said, "Every five hundred years a true king must arise." Now that Your Majesty has emerged in response to the times, are You not that true ruler? Your servant has wiped his eyes in anticipation of this for a long time. Yet I reflect that Your Majesty would surely be unwilling to rank Yourself among the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties; and since You do not wish to be ranked with the Han, Tang, and Song, You must aspire to equal Yao 堯 and Shun 舜. Should You not become like Yao and Shun, not only would Your Majesty's own heart be dissatisfied, it would also be a source of shame to Your servant. What, then, should be done today? It is simply a matter of extending knowledge and investigating things, making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind, and cultivating the person and regulating the family. As for what is called governing the state and bringing peace to the world, one merely takes these principles and puts them into practice—why would one need to seek it in the trivialities of clever schemes and statecraft techniques! Those today who discuss governing the state and bringing peace to the world speak of ensuring sufficient troops and food, replenishing state finances, increasing the registered population, and expanding territory—how could such people be considered skilled at governing and bringing peace? Does the Commentary (of the Great Learning, Daxue) not say: "Possessing virtue, one will possess the people; possessing the people, one will possess the land; possessing the land, one will possess wealth; possessing wealth, one will have resources for use"? What Your servant presents to Your Majesty based on what he has learned is like this; although it may not necessarily be suited to current expediencies, neither is it impractical pedantry. Should it be favored with Your pure perusal, Your servants would be most fortunate, and the world would be most fortunate. Filled with the utmost devotion to his Sovereign, Your servant respectfully braves ten thousand deaths to reply.

translation_en:
Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that supreme filial piety is the essential key to governing All under Heaven, and seeking counsel is the means to fully comprehend the sentiments of All under Heaven. Indeed, the sentiments of All under Heaven are not easily fathomed in full—only by seeking counsel can they be fully comprehended; the vastness of All under Heaven is not easily governed—only through supreme filial piety can it be governed. The Book of Odes (Shijing) says: "Forever he thought of filial piety, and his filial thoughts were the model." Is supreme filial piety not, then, the essential key to governing All under Heaven? It also says: "The ancients had a saying: consult the grass- and firewood-gatherers." Is seeking counsel not, then, the means to fully comprehend the sentiments of All under Heaven?

Reverently I reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed with a nature of keen intelligence and profound wisdom, and possesses the virtues of reverence, frugality, compassion, and benevolence. Formerly, when in the Heir Apparent's Palace, Your reputation for benevolent filiality and Your heroic and resolute plans were already renowned both at court and abroad. Recently, earnestly complying with the testamentary edict of the Late Emperor and graciously yielding to the deepest wishes of Your officials and people, at the very outset of succeeding to the great dynastic mandate, in every governmental ordinance You take only the Imperial Ancestors as Your model, and in every thought and concern You hold only the Late Emperor in Your mind. Your supreme filial piety communicates with the spirits and gods, and Your fine reputation inspires trust far and near. Therefore, throughout the whole world, there is no one who does not look up in admiration to Your Sacred Brilliance, believing that since a ruler capable of great achievements has arisen above, the governance of Grand Peace across All under Heaven will be seen again today. Yet You still do not grow self-satisfied, and have summoned Your servants to the court, broadly issuing a luminous edict to inquire after the Way of ordering the state and pacifying All under Heaven. Looking at myself, Your servant is mediocre and ignorant, without any thorough understanding; yet…

translation_en: … now that Your Sacred Inquiry has descended upon us, how dare I not exhaust all that I hold within to reply! I humbly reflect that Emperor Gao, the Grand Progenitor (Taizu), received the bright mandate of Heaven and came to possess the myriad regions; modeling himself upon the essential way of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, he established grand regulations immutable for ten thousand generations, with canons and rules to bequeath to eternity. As for the Sovereign of Ten Thousand Chariots appearing at the palace verandah to personally put policy questions to the multitude of scholars, this embodies the very same magnificent intention as the ancient august emperors who made clear inquiries of the lower people and delighted in questioning and examining. Emperor Wen, the Grand Ancestor (Taizong), and Emperor Zhao (Renzong) grandly carried this forward before, while Emperor Zhang (Xuanzong) and Emperor Rui (Yingzong) continued and transmitted it after; this is truly a magnificent institution for modeling on antiquity and seeking good governance, one that can be practiced for ahundred million myriad generations without defect. Now Your Majesty, while in the midst of imperial mourning, has reached the day for examining the scholars, neither wishing to abandon the institutions of former reigns nor failing to desire the full expression of filial devotion. Reading the words in Your Majesty's policy question—that "alone and sorrowful in distress, in My feelings I cannot carry this out with an easy heart"—your servant respectfully bows his hands and knocks his head to the ground, knowing thereby that Your Majesty's supreme filial piety can uphold the Imperial Ancestral Temple, can comfort the Late Emperor, can serve the Merciful Sacred Empress Dowager, can make a fourth with the Three Kings and a sixth with the Five Emperors, and can prolong the boundless blessings of the Dynasty for ten thousand times ten thousand years. For filial piety is the constant principle of Heaven, the righteousness of Earth, …

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
民之行立以仁愛誠敬之至盡虞舜之遺善而
而已矣一孝立而萬善從之其於治國平天下
果何難哉昔帝舜備大孝之德而當時庶績有
咸熙之美黎民有於變之風武王有達孝之實
而當時四方以之無思不服天下以之應傒順
德皆此心之推也是則愛敬盡於事親而德教
加于百姓刑于四海誠在

士其各敷陳所蘊以獻務切時宜毋泛毋略朕
將采而行之臣又有以知
陛下聖心孜孜誠欲盡得天下之情而大開求言之

Once filial piety is established, ten thousand virtues follow; what difficulty, then, could there truly be in governing the state and bringing peace to the realm? In antiquity, Emperor Shun possessed the virtue of great filial piety, and in his time there was the beauty of all achievements shining brightly, and the common people had the custom of being transformed for the better; King Wu of Zhou possessed the reality of far-reaching filial piety, and in his time the four quarters because of it never thought of not submitting, and the realm because of it responded to his expectations in accordance with virtue—all of this was the extension of this single mind. Thus, when love and reverence are exhausted in serving one's parents, moral teaching reaches the common people and serves as a model within the Four Seas; this truly lies within a single turn of Your Majesty's mind—what need is there for your servant to speak at length? Yet in Your Majesty's generous intention in guiding your servants to speak, You also declared: "Although We do not appear in person at the palace front to question you in detail, all you numerous scholars shall each set forth what you have stored in your minds and present it; be sure that it addresses the needs of the times, neither vague nor cursory, and We shall select from your words and put them into practice." From this, your servant further knows that Your Majesty's sacred mind is tirelessly diligent, truly wishing to fully grasp the conditions of the realm and throw wide open the avenue for seeking counsel. Receiving the imperial edict, I am moved with gratitude and scarce know what to say. I humbly consider that being solitary in grief and distress is the mind of supreme filial piety, whereas carrying on a predecessor's intentions and continuing his undertakings is the substance of supreme filial piety. Having this mind, one ought to strive after its substance; fulfilling its substance is the very means of fulfilling that mind. I humbly reflect that Your Majesty has ascended the supreme throne of the Late Emperor and received the Late Emperor's charge of the dynasty; how the sun, moon, and stars move in their proper courses, how the Four Seas and Nine Provinces enjoy peace and tranquility, and even how birds, beasts, grasses, and trees all flourish according to their nature—in a single…

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
日二日萬幾皆
陛下繼志述事之所當盡者也臣則不敢泛陳請更
謹條今日初政之首務繼志述事之大端為三
言以獻一曰親正人以正天下二曰謹嗜好以
帥天下三曰勤聖學以臨天下臣伏聞
太宗文皇帝寶訓有曰敬以持己恕以及物親近賢
士屏遠小人是即親正人之謂也又曰毋褻狎
以自流毋縱欲以敗度毋玩物以喪志是即謹
嗜好之謂也又曰玉有美璞不加琱琢之工不
能成宗廟之器人有美質不加學問之力不能
===
知聖賢之道是即勤聖學之謂也自是
列聖相承兢兢業業莫不以此三者為首務而加意
焉
陛下以至孝之心行至孝之實則今日所以繼志述
事而盡治國平天下之道者宜無先於此者臣
請得而熟數之
陛下試垂聽焉夫人君之一身家國天下之本自古
人君之克成聖德未有不本於輔養之力苟輔
養之非人則身不可得而脩矣果何以正天下
乎惟其前後左右罔匪正人則薰陶涵養之盛

translation_en:
… and the myriad affairs of a single day or two days are all matters in which Your Majesty ought to fulfill to the utmost the continuation of his intentions and the carrying forward of his undertakings. Your servant does not dare to offer vague generalizations, and begs instead to respectfully itemize the foremost tasks of today's new administration and the great essentials of continuing his intentions and carrying forward his undertakings, presenting them in three points: first, stay close to upright men in order to rectify the realm; second, be circumspect in desires and preferences in order to lead the realm; third, be diligent in sagely learning in order to rule over the realm. Your servant has humbly heard that the Precious Injunctions (Baoxun) of Emperor Wen, the Grand Ancestor [the Yongle Emperor], state: "Hold fast to oneself with reverence, extend empathy to others, draw close to worthy scholars, and keep petty men at a distance." This is precisely what is meant by staying close to upright men. They also state: "Do not let familiar intimacy lead you into laxity, do not indulge desires to the ruin of proper measure, and do not dally with curiosities to the loss of high purpose." This is precisely what is meant by being circumspect in desires and preferences. They also state: "Though jade be a fine uncarved stone, without applying the craft of carving and polishing, it cannot become a vessel for the ancestral temple; though a person have fine innate qualities, without applying the effort of study and inquiry, he cannot know the Way of the sages and worthies." This is precisely what is meant by being diligent in sagely learning. From that time on, the successive sage emperors inherited the line one after another, cautious and conscientious, and none failed to take these three things as their foremost task and pay special heed to them. Since Your Majesty, with a heart of supreme filial piety, is carrying out the substance of supreme filial piety, then in continuing his intentions and carrying forward his undertakings today so as to fulfill to the utmost the Way of governing the state and bringing peace to the realm, there should be nothing that takes precedence over these. Your servant begs leave to enumerate them thoroughly, if Your Majesty would deign to listen.

Now the ruler's own person is the root of the family, the state, and the realm. Since antiquity, no ruler who was able to bring sagely virtue to completion has ever failed to base it upon the strength of guidance and nurture. If those who guide and nurture him are not the right men, then his own person cannot be cultivated; how then could he rectify the realm? Only when those before and behind him, to his left and to his right, are none other than upright men—so that through the abundance of their moulding influence and nurturing cultivation,…

title: 天順八年進士登科錄
text:
處謇謇諤諤之在侍所聞必正言而非正之言
不得以惑其聰明所見必正事而非正之事不
得以亂其心志所行必正道而非正之道不得
以撓其設施然後出入起居無違禮發號施令
無不善而正天下之道得矣詩曰有馮有翼有
孝有德以引以翼豈弟君子四方為則孟子曰
君仁莫不仁君義莫不義君正莫不正一正君
而國定矣此臣所以願
陛下盡繼述之孝而親正人以正天下也至若人君
之嗜好尤國家治忽之所關自古人君之風化
===
天下未有不本於嗜好之正苟嗜好之不正則
心不正而意不誠矣亦何以帥天下乎惟其一
嗜一好莫非天理則容悅者無自而投其間逢
迎者無自而抵其隙所寶惟賢而聲色貨利之
不干所愛惟民而神仙土木之不事所敬惟天
而干戈刑罰之不黷然後天理之念昭著于宸
極道德之好風化于遠邇而帥天下之道得矣
大學曰未有上好仁而下不好義者也未有好
義其事不終者也孟子曰上有好者下必有甚
焉者矣此臣所以願

Only then will his movements and daily life never violate ritual propriety, his proclamations and commands never fail to be good, and the Way of rectifying the realm be attained. The Book of Odes (Shijing) says: "There are those to rely on, those to assist; those who have filial piety, those who have virtue, to lead and to support. Easy and fraternal is the lord, a model for the four quarters." The Mencius (Mengzi) says: "If the ruler is humane, none will not be humane; if the ruler is righteous, none will not be righteous; if the ruler is upright, none will not be upright. Once the ruler is rectified, the state will be settled." This is why your servant wishes Your Majesty to fulfill the filial piety of carrying on your predecessors' aims and undertakings, and to stay close to upright men in order to rectify the realm. As for the ruler's personal inclinations and desires, they are especially critical to the order or neglect of the state. Since antiquity, no ruler has ever transformed the realm through moral influence without grounding it in the rectitude of his inclinations and desires. If his inclinations and desires are not upright, then his mind will not be upright and his intentions will not be sincere; how then could he lead the realm? Only when every single inclination and desire is nothing other than Heavenly Principle will flatterers have no way to insinuate themselves and sycophants have no gap to exploit. 矣謹嗜好矣則治國平天下之本正矣而非致
勤於
聖學以盡夫格物致知之功則存於心者未能無秋
毫之累形於外者未能無纖芥之惑所親所好
或不能終保其正而亦何以臨天下哉書曰學
于古訓乃有獲詩曰日就月將學有緝熈于光

究王之仁政而未盡行何者為今日之弊端而
未盡革戢以未之信以出之時省而遠行之惟
□實用不事□文至於講明之熟踐履之純則
□□下□□□□盡日用之間□所意欲莫非
□□□□□□□□□□□□志述事之孝
punctuated: 陛下盡繼述之孝，而謹嗜好以帥天下也。既親正人矣，謹嗜好矣，則治國平天下之本正矣。而非致勤於聖學，以盡夫格物致知之功，則存於心者未能無秋毫之累，形於外者未能無纖芥之惑，所親所好或不能終保其正，而亦何以臨天下哉？《書》曰：「學于古訓，乃有獲。」《詩》曰：「日就月將，學有緝熈于光明。」此臣所以又願陛下盡繼述之孝，於山陵畢日，早開經筵，咨訪儒臣，切劘治道，講求二帝三王之政，與討論祖宗列聖之宏規，而監漢、唐、宋以來諸君之得失，熟復於言辭之表，體驗於躬行之間，求其何者為今日之所宜守，何者為今日之所宜戒，何者為先王之仁政而未盡行，何者為今日之弊端而未盡革，敏以求之，信以出之，時省而遠行之，惟務實用，不事空文。至於講明之熟，踐履之純，則一動不□為聖賢，雖日用之間，隨所意欲，莫非天理，則治國平天下□為康獻之準，志述事之孝…
translation_en:
…Your Majesty will fulfill the filial duty of carrying on and continuing the ancestral legacy, and be cautious in Your preferences and desires so as to lead the empire.

Once You have drawn close to upright men and become cautious in Your preferences and desires, the foundation for governing the state and bringing peace to the empire is rectified. Yet unless You apply diligent effort to sagging learning so as to exhaust the work of investigating things and extending knowledge, that which is preserved in the mind cannot be free from the slightest blemish, and that which is manifested externally cannot be free from the tiniest delusion. Those whom You draw close to and that which You favor might not be able to preserve their rectitude to the end—and how then could You preside over the empire? The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Study the ancient lessons, and then you will have attainment." The Book of Odes (Shi) says: "With daily progress and monthly advance, my learning has continuous brightness toward illumination."

This is why Your servant further wishes that Your Majesty will fulfill the filial duty of carrying on and continuing the ancestral legacy by opening the Classics Colloquium early once the imperial mausoleum rites are concluded, consulting with Confucian officials, earnestly honing the Way of governance, investigating the policies of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, discussing the grand plans of Your Ancestors and the successive Sacred Emperors, and taking warning from the successes and failures of the various rulers since the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties. Repeatedly ponder what lies beyond the mere words, and personally experience it in Your own conduct, seeking out what ought to be upheld today, what ought to be guarded against today, what benevolent policies of the former kings have not yet been fully put into practice, and what abuses of the present day have not yet been fully reformed. Seek them with diligence, issue them in good faith, examine them constantly, and carry them out far and wide, devoting Yourself solely to practical application and not engaging in empty words.

When Your elucidation and understanding have become thorough and Your actual practice pure, then not a single movement will fail to [?] be that of a sage or worthy; even in daily affairs, whatever Your mind desires will be nothing other than Heavenly Principle. Then in governing the state and bringing peace to the empire [?], [it will serve as] a standard of peace and excellence [?], and the filial piety of carrying on their aims and continuing their undertakings…

punctuated: 當代□□矣。雖然，愚臣竊以陛下之所躬行，不可以復有加也；而臣子之心，每欲有加無已而望陛下。蓋天之生聖人之材也甚吝，而人之遇聖人之時也甚難。今聖人之材，天旣付畀於陛下；則聖人之澤，人皆望被於此時。此臣所以感陛下求言之實，而盡臣子獻言之誠，惓惓以是三者為繼述之首而敷對焉。非臣一人之私情，實天下願望陛下之至情也。《書》曰：「敬脩其可願。」又曰：「監于先王成憲，其永無愆。」陛下誠采而行之，將見功業逐日以新，聲名随風而流，而有以大慰天下之望矣。愚臣幸甚，天下幸甚，萬世幸甚。臣冒瀆天聰，不勝恐懼之至。謹對。
translation_en: … in the present age [?]. Even so, your foolish servant privately believes that what Your Majesty personally practices cannot be further surpassed; yet the heart of a minister and subject always wishes for endless advancement in its hopes for Your Majesty. For Heaven is most sparing in giving birth to the talent of a sage, and for people to encounter the era of a sage is most difficult. Now that the talent of a sage has already been bestowed by Heaven upon Your Majesty, everyone hopes to receive the beneficence of a sage at this very time. This is why your servant, moved by the sincerity of Your Majesty's request for counsel and exhausting a subject's good faith in offering words, has earnestly set forth this reply with these three matters as the foremost priorities for carrying on the dynastic heritage. This is not the private sentiment of your servant alone, but truly the deepest hope that all under Heaven hold for Your Majesty. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Reverently cultivate what is desirable." It also says: "Take as your mirror the established statutes of the former kings, and you will forever be without fault." If Your Majesty truly selects these words and puts them into practice, we shall see your achievements and enterprises renewed day by day, and your renown flowing with the wind, thereby greatly fulfilling the hopes of all under Heaven. How fortunate for your foolish servant! How fortunate for all under Heaven! How fortunate for ten thousand generations! Having presumptuously imposed upon Your Heavenly Hearing, your servant is overcome with the utmost fear and trepidation. I respectfully reply.
